# Overview

```{r fig.align="right", echo=FALSE, out.width="25%", out.extra='style="float:right; padding:10px"'}
knitr::include_graphics(path = "../man/figures/Symbol.png", error = FALSE)
```

**celliverse** is an R package for single-cell RNA-seq analysis that introduces a family of methods based on **Expression-Weighted Centered Scaled Ranks (EWCSR)**.

The main goals of the package are:

-   High-quality unsupervised and data-driven clustering
-   Discovery of specific positive and negative markers
-   Marker purity evaluation
-   Feature (marker) selection across the entire dataset for dimension reduction and visualization
-   Cell type annotation using CelliVerse Marker DB

<div class="celliverse-note">
<strong>In brief:</strong> CelliVerse provides an integrated workflow for reference-free clustering, marker discovery, marker evaluation, and marker-based cell type annotation in single-cell RNA-seq datasets.
</div>

## What you will learn

In this vignette, you will learn how to:

- Run `clustoCell()` for unsupervised clustering and marker discovery
- Add ClustoCell labels back to a Seurat object
- Select informative dataset-level features for visualization
- Identify and visualize cluster-specific and cell-subset-specific markers
- Assess marker purity
- Annotate cell types using CelliVerse Marker DB
- Scale ClustoCell to large datasets using sketching and label transfer

# **Core Workflows**    

The core functions can be grouped into four main workflows:

## Joint clustering and marker discovery    

-   [clustoCell](#clustoCell) (`clustoCell()`) performs unsupervised clustering of single-cell data using expression-weighted centered scaled ranks (EWCSR), followed by identification of cluster-specific markers and optional sub-clustering.

## Cluster and cell subset marker identification, assessment and visualization    

-   [markoClust](#markoClust) (`markoClust()`) identifies markers in predefined cell clusters, and optionally identifying sub-clusters using Leiden community detection.    

-   [markoCell](#markoCell) (`markoCell()`) identifies and ranks positive and negative marker genes for a specified set of cells, which may correspond to clusters, sub-clusters, arbitrary cell subsets, or even single cells.    

-   [markerPurity](#markerPurity) (`markerPurity()`) quantifies marker purity by evaluating expression specificity within clusters or user-defined cell subsets.    

-   [markoClustVis](#markoClustVis) (`markoClustVis()`) generates a faceted dot plot for visualizing marker genes across clusters, sub-clusters, or cell subsets stored in a ClustoCell or MarkoCell object.

## Cell type annotation    

-   [typoClust](#typoClust) (`typoClust()`) annotates clusters, sub-clusters, or arbitrary cell subsets using curated cell-type marker databases or large language model (LLM)–based annotation.    

-   [typoClustVis](#typoClustVis) (`typoClustVis()`) visualizes cell-type annotation results generated by typoClust.

## Helper and other visualization functions    

-   [addClustoData](#addClustoData) (`addClustoData()`) adds major cluster and/or sub-cluster labels stored in a ClustoCell object to the cell-level metadata of a Seurat or SingleCellExperiment object.    

-   [addTypoData](#addTypoData) (`addTypoData()`) adds inferred cell type annotations from a TypoClust object to the metadata of a Seurat or SingleCellExperiment object.    

-   [getDatasetMarkers](#getDatasetMarkers) (`getDatasetMarkers()`) extracts positive, negative, and/or medium markers from major clusters and sub-clusters stored in a ClustoCell object. These markers could be treated as the dataset-level features for dimension reduction or machine learning purposes.    

-   [clustoCell_TransferLabel](#clustoCell_TransferLabel) (`clustoCell_TransferLabel()`) transfers major and sub-cluster labels from a ClustoCell object generated on a sketched (subsampled) dataset to a full-resolution dataset.    

-   [signatureDotHeatmap](#signatureDotHeatmap) (`signatureDotHeatmap()`) generates a dot heatmap summarizing expression of signature-associated features across clusters.

<div class="celliverse-tip">
<strong>Recommended workflow:</strong> Start with <code>clustoCell()</code> for data-driven clustering and marker discovery, use <code>addClustoData()</code> to add the results back to the dataset, apply <code>markoClust()</code> or <code>markoCell()</code> for focused marker analysis, and then use <code>typoClust()</code> for cell type annotation.
</div>

<a href="#top">Back to top</a>

# Example Workflow

> We will demonstrate the full workflow using the well-known **pbmc3k** dataset (2,700 PBMCs).

**Loading packages and data**

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

library(celliverse)
library(Seurat)
library(patchwork)
library(ggplot2)
library(magrittr)
library(data.table)

# Load the built-in pbmc3k sparse count matrix
data("pbmc3k", package = "celliverse")
```

<div class="celliverse-note">
<strong>Input format:</strong> In this vignette, the example dataset is converted into a Seurat object and analyzed from the raw count matrix. Most CelliVerse functions are designed to work naturally with Seurat-based single-cell workflows.
</div>

Create a Seurat object. You may adjust the thresholds for the initial cell and feature (gene) filtration and perform additional quality checks such as the percentage of mitochondrial DNA.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

pbmc3k_so <- CreateSeuratObject(
  counts = pbmc3k,
  project = "pbmc3k",
  min.cells = 3,
  min.features = 200
)

```

## Running ClustoCell {#clustoCell}

<div class="celliverse-note">
<strong>Conceptual note:</strong> ClustoCell uses expression-weighted centered scaled ranks (EWCSR) to capture within-cell transcriptional structure and identify biologically coherent cell populations without relying on predefined reference labels.
</div>

We will not run the default Seurat clustering here; instead, we demonstrate **celliverse** clustering using *clustoCell* from the beginning.

`clustoCell()` is the main entry point of the package. It performs the following steps:

-   EWCSR transformation\
-   Leiden clustering\
-   Marker discovery\
-   (Optional) sub-clustering

**clustoCell** can perform clustering and marker detection directly on raw data, so you do not need to normalize your data beforehand. You can simply provide your Seurat object as input.

By default, the function uses the **count** layer from the **RNA** assay. If your assay or layer names are different from the standard ones, you can adjust the corresponding arguments.

If you want to use already normalized data (e.g. the *data* layer), make sure to set `log1p = FALSE.` This is important because `log1p` is set to `TRUE` by default and is intended for raw (or any non-log-transformed) data.

```{r, message=FALSE}

pbmc_clustoCell <- clustoCell(
  data            = pbmc3k_so,
  verbose         = FALSE
)

```

Alternatively, you can provide the input data as a matrix (either a base `matrix` or a `dgCMatrix`) instead of a Seurat object.

However, it is recommended to use a sparse matrix of class `dgCMatrix`, as it is more memory-efficient and better suited for large datasets.

```{r, eval=FALSE}

pbmc3k_mat <- pbmc3k_so[["RNA"]]$counts
# Or pbmc3k_mat <- pbmc3k_so[["RNA"]]$counts %>% as.matrix()

pbmc_clustoCell <- clustoCell(
  data            = pbmc3k_mat,
  verbose         = FALSE
)

```

Now let's have a look at the ClustoCell object

```{r, message=FALSE}

print(pbmc_clustoCell)

```

As we see ClustoCell has identified 5 major clusters and 12 sub-clusters. Cells that don’t have ‘high’ markers are filtered out and labeled as quiescent, indicating they are in a resting or inactive state.

<a href="#top">Back to top</a>

## Adding cluster labels to the dataset {#addClustoData}

You can easily add the cluster labels back to your Seurat or SingleCellExperiment object.

By default, both the **major clusters** and **sub-clusters** are added to the object’s metadata as two columns named `"ClustoCell_Clusters"` and `"ClustoCell_SubClusters"`.

You can change these column names if needed, and you can also choose whether to add only major clusters, only sub-clusters, or both by adjusting the corresponding arguments.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

pbmc3k_so <- addClustoData(
  obj         = pbmc3k_so,
  clustoCell  = pbmc_clustoCell
)

```

<a href="#top">Back to top</a>

## Dataset feature selection {#getDatasetMarkers}

<div class="celliverse-tip">
<strong>Tip:</strong> <code>getDatasetMarkers()</code> can be used to select informative dataset-level features before dimensionality reduction and visualization. This provides a CelliVerse-driven alternative to relying only on highly variable genes.
</div>

To visualize the data, you can first perform feature selection as shown below, and then run dimensionality reduction using the selected features (markers), rather than highly variable genes (HVGs).

You can choose to select features based on **major clusters**, **sub-clusters**, or both. You can also decide whether to include **positive**, **negative**, or **medium** markers, or any combination of these.

In addition, you can adjust the threshold for marker selection using the corresponding arguments.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# Performing feature selection
pbmc3k_markers <- getDatasetMarkers(
  obj = pbmc_clustoCell,
  pos_thresh = 85
)

```

We then use the selected features (i.e., `pbmc3k_markers$combined_markers`) as input to the `ScaleData` and `RunPCA` functions.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# Running Seurat pipeline for dimension reduction 
# while using ClustoCell-based selected features

pbmc3k_so <- NormalizeData(pbmc3k_so,
                           normalization.method = "LogNormalize", 
                           scale.factor = 10000)

pbmc3k_so <- ScaleData(pbmc3k_so, 
                       features = pbmc3k_markers$combined_markers)

pbmc3k_so <- RunPCA(pbmc3k_so, npcs = 10, 
                    features = pbmc3k_markers$combined_markers, 
                    reduction.name = "clustoCell_pca")

pbmc3k_so <- RunUMAP(pbmc3k_so, dims = 1:10, 
                     reduction = "clustoCell_pca", 
                     reduction.name = "clustoCell_umap")
```

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# UMAP visualization of major clusters
DimPlot(pbmc3k_so, reduction = "clustoCell_umap", 
        cols = pbmc3k_so$ClustoCell_Clusters %>% 
          unique() %>% 
          length() %>% 
          DiscretePalette(),
        group.by = "ClustoCell_Clusters") + 
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       subtitle = paste0(
         "Based on ",
         length(pbmc3k_markers$combined_markers),
         " features"
       ))

```

The UMAP shows the major ClustoCell populations identified from the EWCSR-based clustering workflow.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# UMAP visualization of sub-clusters
DimPlot(pbmc3k_so, reduction = "clustoCell_umap", 
        cols = pbmc3k_so$ClustoCell_SubClusters %>% 
          unique() %>% 
          length() %>% 
          DiscretePalette(),
        group.by = "ClustoCell_SubClusters") + 
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, 
       subtitle = paste0(
         "Based on ",
         length(pbmc3k_markers$combined_markers),
         " features"
       ))

```

The sub-cluster visualization provides a finer-resolution view of transcriptionally distinct cell states within the major ClustoCell clusters.

<a href="#top">Back to top</a>

## Cluster marker evaluation {#markoClustVis}

You can visualize the top markers for your clusters using the `markoClustVis` function.

You can choose to display **positive**, **negative**, or **medium** markers, or any combination of these. In this example, we show the top positive markers for the major clusters in the pbmc3k dataset.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

markoClustVis(obj = pbmc_clustoCell, 
              desired_sets = paste("C", 1:5, sep = ""))

```

<a href="#top">Back to top</a>

### Identifying cluster markers {#markoClust}

While `clustoCell` performs clustering together with marker detection, most clustering methods do not provide markers for each cluster. The `markoClust` function allows you to identify and rank markers for clusters that you have already defined using other methods.

For example, you may have identified clusters using the Seurat clustering pipeline and want to find the top markers for each cluster to help determine their cell types or subtypes.

By default, `markoClust` will also identify sub-clusters within your clusters while detecting markers (`identify_subclusters = TRUE`). You can change this behavior if needed.

In the example below, we first run the standard Seurat clustering pipeline on the pbmc3k dataset, and then use `markoClust` to identify the top markers for each cluster.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# Running the standard Seurat clustering pipeline
pbmc3k_so <- FindVariableFeatures(pbmc3k_so, 
                                  selection.method = "vst", 
                                  nfeatures = 2000)
pbmc3k_so <- ScaleData(pbmc3k_so)

pbmc3k_so <- RunPCA(pbmc3k_so, npcs = 10)

pbmc3k_so <- FindNeighbors(pbmc3k_so, dims = 1:10,
                           verbose = FALSE)

pbmc3k_so <- FindClusters(pbmc3k_so, resolution = 0.5,
                          verbose = FALSE)

pbmc3k_so <- RunUMAP(pbmc3k_so, dims = 1:10)

# UMAP visualization of sub-clusters
DimPlot(pbmc3k_so, reduction = "umap", 
        group.by = "seurat_clusters") + 
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)

# Running markoClust on Seurat generated clusters (seurat_clusters)
pbmc3k_markoClust <- markoClust(data = pbmc3k_so, 
                                cluster_labels = "seurat_clusters",
                                identify_subclusters = FALSE,
                                verbose = FALSE)

```

Now, let's visualize the top positive markers identified by `markoClust` for the Seurat clusters in the pbmc3k dataset.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

markoClustVis(obj = pbmc3k_markoClust)

```

<a href="#top">Back to top</a>

### Identifying cell subset markers {#markoCell}

In some cases, you may want to find markers for **a specific subset of cells**, rather than for an entire cluster. The `markoCell` function is designed for this purpose and can identify markers for both **user-defined clusters** and **selected cell subsets**.

More generally, `markoCell` is useful whenever you want to study the markers and identity of any selected group of cells.

For example, suppose you cluster the same dataset using both ClustoCell and Seurat, and then compare the results. You may notice that most cells from a Seurat cluster match one ClustoCell cluster, but a small subset of cells is assigned differently.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# Visualizing the confusion matrix of ClustoCell and Seurat clusters
table(pbmc3k_so$seurat_clusters, pbmc3k_so$ClustoCell_Clusters) %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  data.table::setnames(c("Seurat clusters", 
                         "ClustoCell clusters", "Count")) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = `ClustoCell clusters`, 
             y = `Seurat clusters`,  
             fill = Count)) +
  geom_point(size = 5, shape = 21) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Count), vjust = -1) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", 
                       high = scales::muted("#DC0000FF")) +
  theme_minimal()

```

<div class="celliverse-tip">
<strong>Use case:</strong> <code>markoCell()</code> is especially useful for investigating small or ambiguous subsets of cells, such as cells assigned differently by two clustering methods.
</div>

In this example, Seurat cluster 1 contains 500 cells and is annotated as **memory CD4+ T cells** based on its markers. Of these, 475 cells match ClustoCell cluster C3, while 25 cells match ClustoCell cluster C1.

ClustoCell cluster C3 mostly corresponds to Seurat cluster 1 (memory CD4+ T cells), whereas ClustoCell cluster C1 mainly corresponds to Seurat cluster 4 (**CD8+ cytotoxic T cells**). This makes the 25 cells of interest, as they are assigned differently by the two methods.

To better understand their identity, you can use `markoCell` to identify the key markers for this subset and compare them with the markers of ClustoCell clusters C3 and C1, as well as Seurat clusters 1 and 4.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

seurat_1_clustoCell_C1 <- colnames(pbmc3k_so)[pbmc3k_so$seurat_clusters == 1 & pbmc3k_so$ClustoCell_Clusters == "C1"]
length(seurat_1_clustoCell_C1)

pbmc3k_1_C1_markoCell <- markoCell(data = pbmc3k_so, 
                                   desired_cells = list(
                                     "s_1_cc_C1" = seurat_1_clustoCell_C1
                                     ), 
                                   verbose = FALSE)

```

Now let's visualize the top markers of this subset of cells.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

markoClustVis(obj = pbmc3k_1_C1_markoCell)

```

The results show that the top 5 markers of these 25 cells closely match those of Seurat cluster 4 (CD8+ cytotoxic T cells) and ClustoCell cluster C1. This suggests that ClustoCell has more accurately grouped these cells with cytotoxic cells, while Seurat has placed them with memory CD4+ T cells.

<a href="#top">Back to top</a>

### Assessing purity of markers {#markerPurity}

In some cases, you may have a specific marker in mind and want to check how purely it is expressed in a particular cluster or subset of cells. The `markerPurity` function allows you to do this quickly.

It uses the EWCSR framework and Gini coefficient to measure purity, defined as the proportion of cells in the selected group that show high expression of the marker.

For example, you can use `markerPurity` to examine how purely the gene *NKG7* is expressed in Seurat cluster 6.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

pbmc3k_6_NKG7_markerPurity <-
  markerPurity(data = pbmc3k_so, 
               desired_markers = "NKG7", 
               cluster_labels = "seurat_clusters", 
               desired_clusters = "6", 
               verbose = FALSE)

```

```{r}

knitr::kable(pbmc3k_6_NKG7_markerPurity$within_clusters$positive_markers$`6`)

```

<a href="#top">Back to top</a>

## Cell type annotation    

You can annotate clusters, sub-clusters, or any selected group of cells using the **CelliVerse Marker DB**. This is a curated database of positive and negative marker genes for human and mouse, stored in a sparse matrix format. It combines data from several major resources, including Cell Marker Accordion, CellMarker2, DISCO, PanglaoDB, ScTypeDB, and singleCellBase.

### Performing cell type annotation {#typoClust}

To perform cell type annotation, use the `typoClust` function. You can run annotation using marker results stored in **ClustoCell** or **MarkoCell** objects, or by providing your own sets of positive and/or negative markers.

- **Positive markers** are genes that are highly expressed in a specific cell type.
- **Negative markers** are genes that should have low or no expression in that cell type.

You can choose to use only positive markers, only negative markers, or both (default is both).

The `typoClust` function also allows you to annotate multiple ClustoCell and/or MarkoCell objects at once, as long as they come from the same tissue type and disease/healthy condition. When providing objects, you can control how many top markers are used by setting the `thresh` argument (default is 20).

Optionally, you can specify the `tissue` and/or `condition` arguments to perform annotation in a more targeted way, instead of using the entire CelliVerse Marker DB.

You can view the available tissue types and disease conditions as shown below.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, eval=FALSE}

data("tissueCondition_types", package = "celliverse")

# Or tissueCondition_types <- celliverse::tissueCondition_types

head(tissueCondition_types$human$diseased_tissueCondition)

```

```{r, echo=FALSE}

knitr::kable(head(celliverse::tissueCondition_types$human$diseased_tissueCondition))

```

In the example below, we annotate the cell types of the 5 major ClustoCell clusters identified in the pbmc3k dataset.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

clustoCell_pbmc_typoClust <- typoClust(objects = list(pbmc_clustoCell),
                                       desired_sets = paste("C", 1:5, sep = ""),
                                       tissue = c("Blood"), 
                                       verbose = FALSE)

```

Let's have a look at the cell type of C1.

```{r, eval=FALSE}

head(clustoCell_pbmc_typoClust$cell_types$C1[,c("Tissue", "Condition", "CellType", "Combined_Score", "Rank")])

```

```{r, echo=FALSE}

knitr::kable(head(clustoCell_pbmc_typoClust$cell_types$C1[,c("Tissue", "Condition", "CellType", "Combined_Score", "Rank")]))

```

<div class="celliverse-tip">
<strong>Tip:</strong> Custom marker panels are useful when you already have a candidate cell state, subtype, or manually curated marker set and want to query it against CelliVerse Marker DB.
</div>

As mentioned above, you can also provide your own sets of positive and/or negative markers.

For example, suppose you have a list of marker genes (e.g., NKG7, CCL5, GZMA, CTSW, CST7, GNLY, CD99, GZMB, PRF1) that define a specific cell subset or cluster, but you do not have a **ClustoCell** or **MarkoCell** object for it.

In this case, you can use the `typoClust` function to determine which cell type best matches your marker panel.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

my_panel_typoClust <- 
  typoClust(
    desired_pos_markers = list(my_panel = c(
      "NKG7", "CCL5", "GZMA", "CTSW", 
      "CST7", "GNLY", "CD99", "GZMB", "PRF1"
      )),
    tissue = c("Blood"), 
    verbose = FALSE)

```

```{r, eval=FALSE}

head(my_panel_typoClust$cell_types$my_panel[,c("Tissue", "Condition", "CellType", "Combined_Score", "Rank")])

```

```{r, echo=FALSE}

knitr::kable(head(my_panel_typoClust$cell_types$my_panel[,c("Tissue", "Condition", "CellType", "Combined_Score", "Rank")]))

```

### Adding cell type annotations to the dataset {#addTypoData}

After running `typoClust`, you can add the inferred cell type annotations back to your Seurat or SingleCellExperiment object using the `addTypoData` function.

The cell type labels are added to the metadata as new columns, based on the specified clusters or cell subsets. You can include multiple ranked cell type predictions, and optionally refine them to more specific labels by adjusting the `rank_thresh` and `refine_thresh` arguments.

In the example below, we add the cell type annotations for the 5 major ClustoCell clusters (stored in the `clustoCell_pbmc_typoClust` object) back to the PBMC Seurat object.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

pbmc3k_so <- addTypoData(obj = pbmc3k_so, 
                         typoClust = clustoCell_pbmc_typoClust,
                         clusters = c("ClustoCell_Clusters"))

```


<a href="#top">Back to top</a>

### Visualizing cell type annotations {#typoClustVis}

To visualize the cell type annotation results from `typoClust`, you can use the `typoClustVis` function.

In the example below, we display the annotated cell types for the 5 major ClustoCell clusters in the pbmc3k dataset, using the results obtained from `typoClust`.

```{r}

typoClustVis(clustoCell_pbmc_typoClust, 
             order_by = "Cluster")

```

<a href="#top">Back to top</a>

### Visualizing signature expressions {#signatureDotHeatmap}

In some cases, you may have predefined sets of marker genes (signatures) and want to see how strongly each cluster in your dataset expresses these signatures. The `signatureDotHeatmap` function can be used to visualize this as a dot heatmap.

For example, suppose you have five gene signatures representing different cell types:

- **CD4+ T cells (CD4 T)**: IL7R, SELL, NOSIP, AES, RARRES3
- **B cells (B)**: CD79A, CD79B, MS4A1, TCL1A, HLA-DRB1
- **Cytotoxic lymphocytes (CL)**: NKG7, GNLY, GZMA, CST7, PRF1
- **Mononuclear phagocytes (MNP)**: S100A8, S100A9, FCN1, AIF1, LST1
- **Platelets (PLT)**: PPBP, PF4, SDPR, GP9, GPX1

First, create a `row_data` data frame that defines these signatures, as shown below.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

pbmc_row_data <- 
  data.frame(
    Features = c(
      "IL7R", "SELL", "NOSIP", "AES", "RARRES3",
      "CD79A", "CD79B", "MS4A1", "TCL1A", "HLA-DRB1",
      "NKG7", "GNLY", "GZMA", "CST7", "PRF1",
      "S100A8", "S100A9", "FCN1", "AIF1", "LST1",
      "PPBP", "PF4", "SDPR", "GP9", "GPX1"
    ),
    Signature = rep(c(
      "CD4 T",
      "B",
      "CL",
      "MNP",
      "PLT"
    ), each = 5)
  )

```

```{r, eval=FALSE}

head(pbmc_row_data)

```

```{r, echo=FALSE}

knitr::kable(head(pbmc_row_data))

```

Then, you can use `signatureDotHeatmap` to visualize the overall expression of these signatures across the five major ClustoCell clusters in the pbmc3k dataset.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

signatureDotHeatmap(
  seurat_obj = pbmc3k_so,
  cluster_col = "ClustoCell_Clusters",
  row_data = pbmc_row_data, 
  features_col = "Features", 
  signature_col = "Signature")

```

<a href="#top">Back to top</a>

## Running ClustoCell on large datasets {#clustoCell_TransferLabel}

<div class="celliverse-warning">
<strong>Large dataset recommendation:</strong> For datasets with hundreds of thousands to millions of cells, consider using sketching or the decoupled sketching plus label-transfer workflow. This can substantially reduce memory use and runtime while preserving the ability to annotate the full dataset.
</div>

ClustoCell can take longer to run on large single-cell datasets with hundreds of thousands or millions of cells. If you run into memory or performance issues, or simply want to speed up the analysis, you can enable the **sketching** option by setting `sketch = TRUE`.

Sketching is intended as a scalability strategy. It reduces runtime and memory requirements by clustering a representative subset of cells, while label transfer allows the final annotations to be mapped back to the complete dataset.

When sketching is enabled, `ClustoCell` (and `markoClust`) first performs preprocessing and feature filtration on the full dataset. It then creates a smaller sketched dataset, performs clustering and sub-clustering on this subset, and finally transfers the cluster labels back to the full dataset using an internal label transfer step. You can control the size of the sketched dataset using the `sketch_ncells` argument (default is 5000).

In the example below, we run ClustoCell with sketching enabled on the pbmc3k dataset (for simplicity), but the same approach applies to datasets of any size.

```{r, message=FALSE}

pbmc_clustoCell_withSketch <- clustoCell(
  data = pbmc3k_so, 
  sketch = TRUE, 
  sketch_ncells = 1500, 
  identify_subclusters = FALSE,
  verbose = FALSE
)

```

After running ClustoCell, you can add the cluster labels back to the Seurat object and visualize them.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

pbmc3k_so <- addClustoData(
  obj         = pbmc3k_so,
  clustoCell  = pbmc_clustoCell_withSketch, 
  major_cluster_name = "ClustoCell_withSketch", 
  add_sub_clusters = FALSE
)

DimPlot(pbmc3k_so, reduction = "clustoCell_umap", 
        cols = pbmc3k_so$ClustoCell_withSketch %>% 
          unique() %>% 
          length() %>% 
          DiscretePalette(),
        group.by = "ClustoCell_withSketch") + 
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       subtitle = paste0(
         "Based on ",
         length(pbmc3k_markers$combined_markers),
         " features"
       ))

```

You can also compare the results by looking at a confusion matrix between:

- ClustoCell run on the full dataset, and
- ClustoCell run with sketching and label transfer

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

table(pbmc3k_so$ClustoCell_withSketch, pbmc3k_so$ClustoCell_Clusters) %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  data.table::setnames(c("ClustoCell with sketch", 
                         "ClustoCell without sketch", "Count")) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = `ClustoCell without sketch`, 
             y = `ClustoCell with sketch`,  
             fill = Count)) +
  geom_point(size = 5, shape = 21) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Count), vjust = -1) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", 
                       high = scales::muted("#DC0000FF")) +
  theme_minimal()

```

In this example, the results show near-perfect agreement, indicating that sketching provides similar results while being much faster.

<a href="#top">Back to top</a>

### Sub-clustering with sketching

When `identify_subclusters = TRUE`, ClustoCell also detects sub-clusters. If you use this together with `sketch = TRUE`, clustering and sub-clustering are both performed on the sketched data, and the labels are then transferred back to the full dataset.

There is also an optional argument, `refine_transferred_subClusters`, which changes how sub-clusters are assigned:

- If `refine_transferred_subClusters = FALSE` (default), sub-cluster labels are directly transferred from the sketched data.
- If `refine_transferred_subClusters = TRUE`, ClustoCell first transfers **major cluster labels** to the full dataset, and then runs sub-cluster detection separately within each major cluster using the full data.

This refinement step can take more time, but it often improves the quality of sub-clusters. Since sub-clustering is performed within each major cluster (which is much smaller than the full dataset), it is still much faster than running ClustoCell on the entire dataset without sketching.

In the example below, we demonstrate this sub-cluster refinement approach on the pbmc3k dataset.

```{r, message=FALSE}

pbmc_clustoCell_withSketch <- clustoCell(
  data = pbmc3k_so, 
  sketch = TRUE, 
  sketch_ncells = 1500, 
  identify_subclusters = TRUE, 
  refine_transferred_subClusters = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE
)

```

Afterwards, we again add the cluster labels back to the Seurat object and visualize them.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

pbmc3k_so <- addClustoData(
  obj         = pbmc3k_so,
  clustoCell  = pbmc_clustoCell_withSketch, 
  sub_cluster_name = "SubClustoCell_withSketch_refined", 
  add_major_clusters = FALSE
)

DimPlot(pbmc3k_so, reduction = "clustoCell_umap", 
        cols = pbmc3k_so$SubClustoCell_withSketch_refined %>% 
          unique() %>% 
          length() %>% 
          DiscretePalette(),
        group.by = "SubClustoCell_withSketch_refined") + 
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       subtitle = paste0(
         "Based on ",
         length(pbmc3k_markers$combined_markers),
         " features"
       ))

```

Finally, we compare the results using a confusion matrix between:

- Sub-clusters from the full dataset, and
- Refined sub-clusters obtained with sketching

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

table(pbmc3k_so$SubClustoCell_withSketch_refined, pbmc3k_so$ClustoCell_SubClusters) %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>% 
  data.table::setnames(c("Refined SubClustoCell with sketch", 
                         "SubClustoCell without sketch", "Count")) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = `SubClustoCell without sketch`, 
             y = `Refined SubClustoCell with sketch`,  
             fill = Count)) +
  geom_point(size = 5, shape = 21) +
  geom_text(aes(label = Count), vjust = -1) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", 
                       high = scales::muted("#DC0000FF")) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, vjust = 0.8))

```

The results show very high agreement, indicating that sketching with refinement maintains accuracy while improving performance.

<a href="#top">Back to top</a>

### Decoupling sketching and label transfer

<div class="celliverse-tip">
<strong>When to decouple:</strong> Use the built-in <code>sketch = TRUE</code> workflow for moderate-to-large datasets. For very large datasets or limited computational resources, first create a sketched object externally, run <code>clustoCell()</code> only on the sketch, and then transfer labels back to the full dataset.
</div>

As mentioned earlier, when running `clustoCell` or `markoClust` with `sketch = TRUE`, the functions still perform preprocessing and feature filtration on the full dataset before sketching. For very large datasets, this initial step can still be slow and resource-intensive.

In such cases, it is recommended to **separate (decouple) the sketching and label transfer steps**.

In this approach:

1. First, create a smaller dataset by sketching the full data (for example, using Seurat’s `SketchData` function).
2. Then, run `clustoCell` on the sketched dataset only. This avoids preprocessing and feature selection on the full dataset.
3. Finally, transfer the cluster labels from the sketched data back to the full dataset using `clustoCell_TransferLabel` and `addClustoData` functions.

The `clustoCell_TransferLabel` function returns an updated **ClustoCell** object including cluster labels for the full dataset.

This strategy is especially useful when working with very large datasets or limited computational resources.

In the example below, we demonstrate this approach using the pbmc3k dataset. Since the full dataset is in the form of raw counts, we use the `"count-project"` method for label transfer.

```{r, message=FALSE, eval=FALSE}

# Sketching the data
set.seed(121) 
pbmc3k_so <- SketchData(
  object = pbmc3k_so,
  assay = "RNA",
  ncells = 1500,
  method = "Uniform",
  sketched.assay = "sketch", 
  verbose = F
)

# Running clustoCell
sketched_pbmc_clustoCell <- clustoCell(
  data = pbmc3k_so,
  assay = "sketch", 
  verbose = FALSE
)

# Converting the ClustoCell object to full dataset mode
sketched_pbmc_clustoCell <- 
  clustoCell_TransferLabel(
    clustoCell = sketched_pbmc_clustoCell, 
    query_expr_mat = pbmc3k_so, 
    assay = "RNA",
    method = "count-project")

# Transferring the labels to the full dataset
pbmc3k_so <- addClustoData(
  obj         = pbmc3k_so,
  clustoCell  = sketched_pbmc_clustoCell,
  major_cluster_name = "sketched_ClustoCell",
  sub_cluster_name = "sketched_SubClustoCell"
)

```
